identity.title: Policy Learning from Tutorial Books via Understanding, Rehearsing and Introspecting

problem.claim: Policy Learning from tutorial Books (PLfB) aims to derive a policy network from tutorial books using LLM-based systems.

gap.claim: Existing decision-making research such as reinforcement learning primarily relies on numerous real-environment interactions and does not use knowledge summarized in text.

contributions.claim: Introduces the PLfB problem for leveraging tutorial books to derive policy networks.

Proposes the three-stage Understanding, Rehearsing, and Introspecting (URI) framework: understand books, rehearse decision trajectories, and distill a policy network through introspection on imaginary data.
Builds PLfB benchmarks based on Tic-Tac-Toe and Football games.

stated_novelty.claim: The paper presents PLfB as a new policy-learning problem centered on deriving policies from tutorial books with LLM-based systems.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that URI achieved at least a 44% net win rate against GPT-based agents without real data.
In Football, the authors report that URI beat built-in AIs with a reported 37%, without explicitly naming that percentage's metric; a GPT-based agent achieved a 6% winning rate.

narrative_sequence.summary: Humans can acquire skills from written books, but decision-making research has mainly depended on real-environment interaction.
The paper formulates PLfB to use tutorial-book knowledge for policy derivation, drawing on LLM systems.
URI understands books, rehearses imagined decision trajectories, and introspects over the resulting imaginary data to distill a policy network.
The authors construct Tic-Tac-Toe and Football benchmarks and report at least a 44% net win rate against GPT-based agents without real data, followed by a separate Football comparison.

source_observation.claim: The abstract explicitly aligns each URI stage with a learning activity: book understanding, trajectory rehearsal, and introspection-based policy distillation.

lessons.interpretation: A staged mapping from an informal learning analogy to concrete computational operations can make a framework's mechanism easier to follow.
lessons.application: When proposing an analogy-inspired method, map each conceptual stage to a specific data transformation or model operation and state the sequence explicitly.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the analogy does not correspond to distinct, testable computational steps.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the benchmark sizes, baselines beyond those named, evaluation protocol, or uncertainty around the reported win rates.
It does not describe the tutorial books, policy architecture, or how imaginary trajectories and introspection are implemented.
